steps.title: The unfinished text
paragraphs: Dev got a text from his sister: “Because the car broke down.”
He stared at it. Because the car broke down… what? Was she late? Was dinner cancelled? Was she stuck on the highway?
Ten minutes later: “Sorry! Meant to say I’ll be late because the car broke down.”
A fragment is like that first text. It starts a thought and leaves the reader to guess the rest.

cards.title: What is a fragment?
cards.body: A fragment is a group of words that starts with a capital and ends with a full stop but isn’t a complete sentence. It is missing a subject, a verb or a finished thought.

cards.title: Four common fragments
cards.text:
No verb: The best day of the summer.
No subject: Jumped over the fence and ran.
Dependent clause alone: Because the bus was late. / Which made us laugh.
Added detail alone: Especially the chocolate ones. / For example, the bake sale.
cards.note: Read each sentence by itself. If it leaves you asking “what about it?” or “who did?”, it’s a fragment.

cards.title: Two ways to fix one
cards.text:
Join it: We stayed inside. Because it was storming. → We stayed inside because it was storming.
Complete it: Running through the rain. → I was running through the rain.
cards.note: Most fragments belong to the sentence right before or after them. Joining is often the quickest fix.

cards.title: What about stories?
cards.body: Authors sometimes use a fragment on purpose for effect (“Silence. Then a scream.”). In essays and reports, write complete sentences.

prompts: Which kind of fragment do you write most often? How will you catch it?
Did the Coach find a fragment in your paragraph? How did you fix it?
